newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Last Moslem refugee house torched in Serb land.
newsitem.headline: Last Moslem refugee house torched in Serb land.

text.p: Serbs have burned the last of a cluster of 15 Moslem houses in a Bosnian village which had been awaiting the arrival of its pre-war Moslem resettlers, a NATO spokesman said on Wednesday.

Ten of the pre-fabricated houses, put up by Moslem refugees from the northeastern village of Gajevi, were razed on March 1 by a mob of 150 Serbs who ignored a patrol of Russian peacekeeping troops. Four other houses were blown up previously.
A group of 30 Serbs went into Gajevi on Tuesday afternoon and threw petrol bombs at the last remaining house, NATO said.
"One house survived, but was seriously damaged and was still standing, so they went back and did a more thorough job yesterday," Major Tony White told Reuters.
The village of Gajevi lies in a former frontline area called the Zone of Separation (ZOS) between Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and the Serb republic, but on the Serb side of the line.
NATO imposed a seven-day restriction of movement in the Gajevi area after the first incident, but the ban was lifted two days ago.
"This type of organised attack is a smack in the face of all authorities responsible for this, including the Stabilisation Force (SFOR)," White said.
"People who do these things know that they can get away with it," he added, reprimanding the Serb police for not even showing up for an investigation organised by the international police.

The destruction of the 15 houses has left Moslem refugees outraged that the NATO force could not protect homes which had been constructed under rules set down by NATO and other international agencies in Bosnia.
They complained of being betrayed by NATO troops who are charged with the overall security in the ZOS, giving them confidence to rebuild their shattered houses.

"We shall go back to our homes even if it means fighting for them," said Sefika Arnautovic, 63. She said the houses were purchased by refugees from a local furniture company at about 15,000 German Marks ($8,800) a piece.

Refugees who were displaced during the Bosnian war have only been returning to areas where they form a majority, aid workers say. Some 220,000 have returned since the end of hostilities in November 1995.

The 600-odd Moslems living in the villages of Dugi Dio, Jusici and Mahala, whose example the Gajevi refugees hoped to follow, present the only minority resettlers in Serb-controlled territory, aid officials say.
